chunks: "I'd start from the performance equation: execution time equals instruction count times cycles per instruction times clock period. Every technique attacks one of those.

To reduce the clock period you shorten the logic per stage, mainly by deeper pipelining, plus better process technology, but frequency costs power roughly cubically because voltage rises with frequency, so it's mostly capped.
To reduce CPI you keep the pipeline busy.

Pipelining gets you toward one instruction per cycle; superscalar designs issue several per cycle; out-of-order execution reorders around dependencies and cache misses; branch prediction avoids flushing the pipeline; and caches, prefetchers and bigger buffers cut the time waiting for memory, which is often the biggest part of CPI.
To reduce instruction count you use a good compiler and ISA features like SIMD or fused instructions, so one instruction does more work.
Then there's parallelism beyond one instruction stream: SIMD or vector units, multithreading like SMT, multiple cores, and specialized accelerators.

The trade-offs are power and area, since wider cores and bigger predictors cost energy, memory bandwidth, which doesn't scale as fast as compute, and Amdahl's law, since only the parallel portion speeds up.
So I'd profile first to see whether the workload is compute-bound or memory-bound, then pick the technique."
